draft.title: Matching equations to graphs
card: Look at where \(x\) sits in the equation. \(y = mx + c\) is a straight line, \(y = ax^{2} + bx + c\) is a parabola, and an equation with \(x^{3}\) as its highest power, such as \(y = x^{3} - 4x\), is a cubic.
A hyperbola has \(x\) under a fraction bar, as in \(y = \frac{k}{x}\). A circle has both \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\), as in \(x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}\).

An exponential has \(x\) in the power, as in \(y = 2^{x}\). When the base is more than 1, it rises to the right, gets close to the \(x\)-axis on the left without touching it, and crosses the \(y\)-axis at \((0, 1)\).
Use the shape to check. A parabola has one turn and both ends go the same way. A cubic has ends that go in opposite directions. Putting \(x = 0\) into the equation gives the \(y\)-intercept.
draft.remember: Match the equation by where \(x\) sits, then check the graph's shape and intercept.

a.q: Which equation gives an exponential graph?
a.why: In \(y = 3^{x}\) the \(x\) is in the power, so the graph is an exponential. In \(y = x^{3}\) the \(x\) is the base and the power is fixed, which makes a cubic.
a.clue: Which one has \(x\) up in the power?

b.q: A graph crosses the \(y\)-axis at 1. It rises steeply to the right and gets close to the \(x\)-axis on the left without touching it. Which equation fits?
b.why: \(y = 2^{x}\) is an exponential with base more than 1. It passes through \((0, 1)\) and gets close to the \(x\)-axis on the left. The other three also cross the \(y\)-axis at 1, but a parabola, a cubic and a line never get close to the \(x\)-axis on one side and stay above it.
b.clue: Crossing at 1 is not enough. Think about the left-hand end.
